title: Non-equilibrium Symmetry Of Cyclic First-passage Times
authors: Shiling Liang And Simone Pigolotti Daniel Maria Busiello
abstract: We study the sum of first passage times along an arbitrary cycle made up of states of a small physical system. We show that, if the system is at thermodynamic equilibrium, this sum follows the same probability distribution regardless of whether the cycle is explored clockwise or counterclockwise (CCW). Out of equilibrium, the distributions of clockwise and CCW cyclic first passage times are related by a detailed fluctuation theorem. This result descends from a symmetry of clockwise and CCW trajectories, which combines time reversal with swapping portions of the trajectories. We then relate the entropy produced along the cycle with the entropy production of the whole system using large deviation theory. Our results reveal a novel symmetry in stochastic systems, of potential broad applicability in non-equilibrium physics.
tldr: The paper discovers a symmetry in cyclic first-passage times that yields a detailed fluctuation theorem relating clockwise and counterclockwise distributions, linking entropy production along a cycle to the total entropy production.
motivation: To understand non-equilibrium symmetries in stochastic systems and derive thermodynamic constraints on first-passage times.
method: The authors analyze the sum of first-passage times along a cycle in a Markovian system, using time-reversal symmetry and large deviation theory to relate distributions and entropy production.
result: At equilibrium, clockwise and counterclockwise cyclic first-passage times are identically distributed; out of equilibrium, they obey a detailed fluctuation theorem. The entropy produced along the cycle is connected to the total entropy production via large deviation theory.
conclusion: The revealed symmetry provides a novel thermodynamic constraint on first-passage times, with broad applicability in non-equilibrium physics.

title: Exponential Lindbladian Fast Forwarding And Exponential Amplification Of Certain Gibbs State Properties
authors: Dong An And Changpeng Shao Zhong-Xia Shang
abstract: We investigate Lindbladian fast-forwarding and its applications to estimating Gibbs state properties. Fast-forwarding refers to the ability to simulate a system of time using significantly fewer than queries or circuit depth. While various Hamiltonian systems are known to circumvent the no fast-forwarding theorem, analogous results for dissipative dynamics, governed by Lindbladians, remain largely unexplored. We first present a quantum algorithm for simulating purely dissipative Lindbladians with unitary jump operators, achieving additive query complexity up to error , improving previous algorithms. When the jump operators have certain structures (i.e. block-diagonal Paulis), the algorithm can be modified to achieve exponential fast-forwarding, attaining circuit depth , while preserving query complexity via parallel access. Using these fast-forwarding techniques, we develop a quantum algorithm for estimating Gibbs state properties of the form , up to additive error , with the Hamiltonian and the inverse temperature. For input states exhibiting certain coherence conditions—e.g. —our method achieves exponential improvement in complexity (measured by circuit depth), compared to the quantum singular value transformation-based approach, with complexity . We show how to apply this exponential improvement to applications such as the ground state overlap testing and amplitude estimation. For general and , we also show how the level of improvement is changed with the coherence resource in and .
tldr: This paper presents quantum algorithms for fast-forwarding Lindbladian evolution and using them to exponentially improve the estimation of Gibbs state properties under certain coherence conditions.
motivation: Simulating dissipative quantum dynamics and estimating Gibbs state properties are central to quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics, but existing methods suffer from high complexity. Fast-forwarding Lindbladians could dramatically reduce circuit depth.
method: The authors develop a quantum algorithm for simulating purely dissipative Lindbladians with unitary jump operators, achieving additive query complexity. For structured jump operators (e.g., block-diagonal Paulis), they modify the algorithm to achieve exponential fast-forwarding in circuit depth while preserving query complexity via parallel access.
result: The algorithm achieves exponential improvement in circuit depth for estimating Gibbs state properties when the input state satisfies certain coherence conditions (e.g., being a computational basis state). This improvement is applied to ground state overlap testing and amplitude estimation.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that exponential fast-forwarding is possible for certain dissipative dynamics, leading to significant speedups for Gibbs state property estimation, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics.

title: Most Incompatible Measurements And Sum-of-squares Optimisation
authors: Sébastien Designolle
abstract: Measurement incompatibility, or joint measurability, is a cornerstone of quantum theory and a useful resource. For finite-dimensional systems, quantifying this resource and establishing universal bounds valid for all measurements is a long-standing problem. In this work, we exhibit analytical universal parent measurements giving access to bounds that beat the state of the art. In particular, we can show that, for relevant robustnesses, sets of anticommuting observables give rise to the most incompatible dichotomic measurements. We also formalise the construction of such universal parent measurements in the framework of sum-of-squares optimisation and obtain preliminary numerical results demonstrating the power of the method by improving on our own analytical values. All results find direct application for demonstrating genuine high-dimensional steering, that is, certifying the dimensionality of a quantum system in a one-sided device-independent manner.
tldr: This paper identifies the most incompatible measurements using sum-of-squares optimization, with applications to high-dimensional steering.
motivation: Quantifying measurement incompatibility and establishing universal bounds is a long-standing problem in quantum theory.
method: The authors construct analytical universal parent measurements and formalize the construction using sum-of-squares optimization.
result: They show that anticommuting observables yield the most incompatible dichotomic measurements, and numerical results improve on analytical bounds.
conclusion: The results provide direct applications for certifying high-dimensional quantum steering in a one-sided device-independent manner.

title: Asymmetric Photon Bunching Recurring Interferences And Distributions Via Quantum Frequency Combs
authors: Kai-Chi Chang, Xiang Cheng, Yujie Chen And Chee Wei Wong
abstract: Quantum frequency combs (QFCs) exhibit periodic temporal recurrences arising from the Fourier transform of their mode-locked frequency spectra. While QFCs have been experimentally demonstrated, asymmetric Hong–Ou–Mandel (HOM) revival interference in QFCs has not been systematically investigated, and the efficient distribution of photon-bunching revivals has remained unreported. Here, we present the first experimental observation and distribution of asymmetric HOM recurrence interference using QFCs. First, we verified HOM revivals spanning 10 time-bins in a 10.21 GHz QFC, obtaining a 72.95 ± 0.8% visibility for its central dip. Then, we measured up to 20 time-bins from a 50 GHz QFC, with an accidental-subtracted central HOM dip visibility of 70.82 ± 0.7%. Finally, we distributed the QFC after 21 km optical fibers without dispersion compensation, observing photon bunching measurements across 12 time-bins, with a central dip visibility of 70.5 ± 0.9%. The deviation from ideal HOM interference is attributed to residual frequency distinguishability between the signal and idler photons, as confirmed in our theoretical calculations. These results establish QFCs as a viable platform for advanced quantum information processing tasks, such as high-dimensional entanglement swapping and quantum communication testbeds.
tldr: First experimental observation and distribution of asymmetric Hong-Ou-Mandel revival interference using quantum frequency combs over 21 km fiber.
motivation: Quantum frequency combs (QFCs) are promising for high-dimensional quantum information processing, but asymmetric HOM revival interference and efficient distribution of photon-bunching revivals had not been systematically investigated.
method: The authors generate QFCs with 10.21 GHz and 50 GHz repetition rates, measure HOM revivals across multiple time-bins, and distribute the QFC over 21 km of optical fiber without dispersion compensation.
result: They observe HOM revivals spanning up to 20 time-bins with visibilities around 70%, and after 21 km fiber distribution, they still observe photon bunching across 12 time-bins with 70.5% visibility.
conclusion: QFCs are a viable platform for advanced quantum information processing tasks such as high-dimensional entanglement swapping and quantum communication testbeds.

title: Observation Of Phase Doubling And Entanglement In Coherent Matter-wave Reactions
authors: Shu Nagata, Tadej Mežnaršič, Chuixin Kong And Cheng Chin
abstract: Chemical reactions in a statistical ensemble are conventionally regarded as incoherent processes driven by thermodynamics. In the quantum degenerate regime, where atoms and molecules form coherent matter waves, reactions are theoretically described by nonlinear mixing of matter-wave fields. In this scenario, we expect phase matching between reactants and products, analogous to the mixing of photonic fields in nonlinear optics. Here we report on the observation of phase coherent reaction dynamics of Bose-condensed atoms and molecules near a Feshbach resonance. Using matter-wave diffraction with optical lattices, we verify spatial coherence of both atoms and molecules and observe phase doubling when atomic waves combine into molecular waves, the matter-wave analogue of optical frequency doubling. The diffraction patterns further reveal two-atom entanglement generated during the reaction. Our observations establish phase coherence and entanglement generation as two essential features of ‘quantum many-body chemistry’. Moreover, our work opens a pathway to control of reaction dynamics by manipulation of matter-wave phases.
tldr: Observation of phase doubling and entanglement in coherent matter-wave reactions of Bose-condensed atoms and molecules near a Feshbach resonance.
motivation: To demonstrate phase coherence and entanglement generation in chemical reactions in the quantum degenerate regime, analogous to nonlinear optics.
method: Matter-wave diffraction with optical lattices to verify spatial coherence and observe phase doubling; analysis of diffraction patterns to infer entanglement.
result: Phase doubling observed when atomic waves combine into molecular waves; diffraction patterns reveal two-atom entanglement generated during the reaction.
conclusion: Establishes phase coherence and entanglement as key features of quantum many-body chemistry, enabling control of reaction dynamics via matter-wave phases.

title: Nonequilibrium Dimension-raising Phase Transitions
authors: Zhizhen Chen And Zi Cai
abstract: We propose a periodically driven system whose dimensionality is an emergent property that can be tunable, thus enables us to realize not only many-body phases with arbitrary dimensions, but also phase transitions, instead of crossovers, between phases with various dimensions. We study an interacting rotor model whose instantaneous Hamiltonian keeps the one-dimensional feature at any given time. Despite this, an emergent two-dimensional (2D) phase appears when the driving frequency exceeds a critical value, at which a dimension-raising phase transition takes place. We find that the nonequilibrium feature of the system could qualitatively change the finite temperature critical behavior of the emergent 2D phase and make it different from its equilibrium counterpart. A four-dimensional generalization and experimental realizations of the proposed model based on a programmable reconfiguration technique in optical tweezers setups have also been discussed.
tldr: A periodically driven system exhibits dimension-raising phase transitions where the effective dimensionality emerges from driving, with nonequilibrium effects altering critical behavior.
motivation: To explore how periodic driving can induce phase transitions between phases of different effective dimensionality, and to study the nonequilibrium critical behavior of such emergent phases.
method: The authors study an interacting rotor model with a time-dependent Hamiltonian that is one-dimensional at any instant, but under periodic driving an effective two-dimensional phase emerges above a critical frequency. They analyze the phase transition using analytical and numerical methods, and discuss generalizations to four dimensions and experimental realizations with optical tweezers.
result: A dimension-raising phase transition occurs at a critical driving frequency, and the finite-temperature critical behavior of the emergent 2D phase differs from its equilibrium counterpart due to nonequilibrium effects.
conclusion: Periodic driving can be used to realize phases with tunable effective dimensionality and phase transitions between them, with unique nonequilibrium critical phenomena.

title: Subgap Pumping Of Antiferromagnetic Mott Insulators: Photoexcitation Mechanisms And Applications
authors: Radu Andrei, Mingyao Guo, Mustafa G Ali, Hoon Kim, Richard D Averitt, David Hsieh And Eugene Demler
abstract: We study the behavior of the 2D repulsive Hubbard model on a square lattice at half filling, under strong driving with ac electric fields, by employing a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach. Within the same theoretical framework, we analytically obtain the conventional Keldysh crossover between multiphoton and tunneling photoexcitation mechanisms, as well as two new regimes beyond the Keldysh paradigm. We discuss how dynamical renormalization of the Mott–Hubbard gap feeds back into the photoexcitation process, modulating the carrier generation rate in real time. The momentum distribution of quasiparticle excitations immediately after the drive is calculated, and shown to contain valuable information about the generation mechanism. Finally, we discuss experimental probing of the pump-induced nonequilibrium electronic state.
tldr: This paper studies photoexcitation mechanisms in antiferromagnetic Mott insulators under strong ac driving, revealing new regimes beyond the Keldysh crossover.
motivation: Understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated systems is important for both fundamental physics and potential applications in ultrafast control of materials.
method: The authors use a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach to analyze the 2D repulsive Hubbard model at half filling under strong ac electric fields.
result: They analytically derive the conventional Keldysh crossover and identify two new photoexcitation regimes, showing that dynamical renormalization of the Mott gap modulates carrier generation in real time.
conclusion: The momentum distribution of quasiparticles after the drive encodes information about the generation mechanism, and experimental probes can access the non-equilibrium electronic state.

title: Quantum Entanglement, Stratified Spaces, And Topological Matter: Towards Entanglement-sensitive Langlands Data
authors: Kazuki Ikeda And Steven Rayan
abstract: Using the spinless Haldane model, we study the witness-filtered Berry curvature, quantum geometric tensor, and quantum Fisher information on the gapped strata of the parameter space and evaluate them through the Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki discretization. The filtered quantities isolate the part of the geometric response carried by sublattice coherence: they suppress contributions from regions where the occupied Bloch state is locally A/B-separable and emphasize regions where curvature and coherence coexist. We derive exact lattice identities, reconstruction formulas for the curvature-weighted coherence, and bounds relating the filtered quantum geometric tensor and quantum Fisher information to single-particle mode entanglement. Across the gap-closing stratum, the quantized response changes admit a natural description in terms of Hecke modifications. We elicit a corresponding Langlands viewpoint—not as a full correspondence, but as an organizational principle and as the mathematical shadow of these physical geometric constructions.
tldr: The paper uses geometric and information-theoretic quantities to study entanglement in topological matter, connecting to Langlands theory.
motivation: To understand how quantum entanglement manifests in topological phases and to develop a mathematical framework linking geometry, information, and topology.
method: Applies witness-filtered Berry curvature, quantum geometric tensor, and quantum Fisher information to the Haldane model, using Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki discretization.
result: Derives exact lattice identities and bounds relating filtered geometric quantities to single-particle mode entanglement, and interprets quantized changes via Hecke modifications.
conclusion: The work suggests a Langlands-inspired organizational principle for entanglement in topological matter, but remains a mathematical exploration rather than a direct contribution to quantum information theory.

title: Symmetry-induced Logarithmic Relaxation In The Quantum Kicked Rotor
authors: Julien Hébraud, Floriane Arrouas, Bruno Peaudecerf, Juliette Billy, David Guéry-Odelin, Olivier Giraud, Bertrand Georgeot, Gabriel Lemarié And Christian Miniatura
abstract: We study the effect of discrete symmetries on coherent multiple scattering in the quantum kicked rotor. When the initial momentum is set to zero—as in recent Bose–Einstein condensate experiments—the effective pseudo-disorder becomes even under momentum inversion. The resulting discrete mirror symmetry of the dynamics profoundly alters spectral correlations: it generates quasi-degenerate Floquet doublets localised at opposite momenta, whose exponentially small splittings produce a hierarchy of exponentially large dynamical timescales. The coherent backscattering and forward-scattering peaks then exhibit a striking non-monotonic evolution and strongly asymmetric contrasts, followed by an exceptionally slow logarithmic relaxation toward a common asymptotic value—a hallmark of glassy dynamics, here emerging in a fully coherent quantum system. That such archetypal glass-like behaviour arises from a single discrete symmetry constraint reveals an unexpected and deep connection between quantum coherence and slow relaxation phenomena.
tldr: This paper shows that discrete mirror symmetry in the quantum kicked rotor leads to glassy logarithmic relaxation, linking symmetry to slow dynamics.
motivation: To understand how discrete symmetries affect coherent multiple scattering and spectral correlations in a paradigmatic quantum chaotic system.
method: Theoretical analysis of the quantum kicked rotor with zero initial momentum, using Floquet theory and symmetry arguments to compute spectral statistics and dynamical observables.
result: Mirror symmetry creates quasi-degenerate Floquet doublets with exponentially small splittings, causing non-monotonic coherent backscattering and forward-scattering peaks and an extremely slow logarithmic relaxation.
conclusion: A single discrete symmetry can produce glassy dynamics in a fully coherent quantum system, revealing a deep connection between symmetry and slow relaxation.

title: Optimizing Qubo On A Quantum Computer By Mimicking Imaginary Time Evolution
authors: Yahui Chai And Alice Di Tucci
abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum–classical algorithm for solving quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems using an imaginary time evolution-mimicking circuit (ITEMC). The circuit parameters are optimized to mimic short-time ITE, using only single- and two-qubit expectation values. This significantly reduces the measurement overhead by avoiding full energy evaluation. By updating the initial state based on results from last step iteratively, the algorithm quickly converges to the low-energy solutions. With a pre-sorting step that optimizes quantum gate ordering based on QUBO coefficients, the convergence is further improved. Our classical simulations achieve approximation ratios above up to 150 qubits. Furthermore, the linear scaling of entanglement entropy with system size suggests that the circuit is challenging to simulate classically using tensor networks. We also demonstrate hardware runs on IBM’s device for 40, 60, and 80 qubits, and obtain solutions compatible with that from simulated annealing.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for solving QUBO problems using a circuit that mimics imaginary time evolution.
motivation: QUBO problems are important for combinatorial optimization, but current quantum algorithms require many measurements or deep circuits.
method: The algorithm optimizes a parameterized circuit to mimic short-time imaginary time evolution using only single- and two-qubit expectation values, avoiding full energy evaluation, and iteratively updates the initial state.
result: Classical simulations achieve high approximation ratios for up to 150 qubits, and hardware runs on IBM devices for up to 80 qubits yield solutions comparable to simulated annealing.
conclusion: The proposed method reduces measurement overhead and converges quickly, but the paper focuses on optimization rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Hybrid Monte Carlo For Fractional Quantum Hall States
authors: Ting-Tung Wang, Ha Quang Trung, Qianhui Xu, Min Long, Bo Yang And Zi Yang Meng
abstract: We develop a hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) method to efficiently compute the physical observables from the samplings of the Laughlin and the Moore–Read (MR) wave functions of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) systems. With the advancements in methodology, including global updates and double stereographic projection on spherical geometry, our HMC simulation is significantly faster than the widely used Metropolis Monte Carlo scheme. As a result, we can readily simulate systems with electron numbers on both disk and sphere geometries. We apply this method to investigate the topological shift obtained from the edge dipole moment, computed from the wave function density on the disk. We also numerically computed the non-Abelian braiding matrices for different braiding schemes of the MR quasiholes on the sphere. Results with much better quality compared with previous works have been achieved. With the thermodynamic limit results obtained at ease, we also discuss the future usage of our method to clarify the questions on the instability of FQH states in an ideal Chern band setting or under quantum decoherence.
tldr: Develops a hybrid Monte Carlo method for simulating fractional quantum Hall wave functions, focusing on computational efficiency and topological properties.
motivation: Efficiently compute observables from Laughlin and Moore-Read wave functions for large systems, overcoming limitations of standard Metropolis Monte Carlo.
method: Hybrid Monte Carlo with global updates and double stereographic projection on spherical geometry, applied to disk and sphere geometries.
result: Significantly faster simulations enabling study of topological shift and non-Abelian braiding matrices with improved quality.
conclusion: The method facilitates thermodynamic limit studies and can address questions on FQH state stability in Chern bands or under decoherence.

title: Anisotropic Fluorescence Signals Retarded Dipole-dipole Interactions In A Thermal Atomic Cloud
authors: Vyacheslav Shatokhin, Friedemann Landmesser, Mario Niebuhr, Frank Stienkemeier, Andreas Buchleitner And Lukas Bruder
abstract: We experimentally observe and theoretically explain anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals in the fluorescence from dilute thermal potassium vapours, at room temperature and particle densities . We identify the retarded part of the geometrically fully resolved inter-atomic, resonant dipole-dipole interaction as the crucial ingredient to theoretically reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
tldr: Experimental and theoretical study of anisotropic fluorescence signals from thermal atomic vapors due to retarded dipole-dipole interactions.
motivation: To understand the role of retarded dipole-dipole interactions in anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals observed in fluorescence from dilute thermal atomic clouds.
method: Experimental observation of fluorescence from thermal potassium vapors combined with theoretical modeling that includes the retarded part of the resonant dipole-dipole interaction.
result: The retarded dipole-dipole interaction is crucial to reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
conclusion: Retarded interactions must be considered to fully explain anisotropic fluorescence signals in thermal atomic ensembles.

title: Analytical Response Functions For A Compressible Thin Fluid Layer With Odd Viscosity *
authors: Yuto Hosaka And Shigeyuki Komura Abdallah Daddi-Moussa-Ider
abstract: Fluids composed of chiral active components can exhibit odd viscosity, a property that breaks time-reversal and parity symmetries. We investigate the hydrodynamic response to monopole and dipole singularities in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, supported by a conventional lubrication layer. Using the two-dimensional Green’s function in Fourier space, we derive analytical solutions for the flow and pressure fields. These solutions provide a detailed description of the hydrodynamic interactions governing the motion of colloidal particles and microswimmers in confined chiral fluids, offering insight into the role of odd viscosity in modifying particle dynamics and collective behavior. The derived results are directly applicable to modeling transport, control, and self-organization phenomena in active and chiral microfluidic systems.
tldr: This paper studies hydrodynamic response functions in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, focusing on chiral active fluids.
motivation: Odd viscosity arises in chiral active fluids and affects particle dynamics and collective behavior; understanding it is important for modeling microfluidic systems.
method: The authors use two-dimensional Green's functions in Fourier space to derive analytical solutions for flow and pressure fields under monopole and dipole singularities.
result: Analytical expressions for the hydrodynamic response are obtained, showing how odd viscosity modifies the flow and pressure fields.
conclusion: The results provide a framework for understanding transport and self-organization in chiral active fluids, with potential applications in microfluidics.

title: Percolation With Coupled Lasers: Effect Of Non-linearities On The Phase Transition
authors: Simon Mahler, Nikita Stroev, Mahmoud Abu Rmilah, Asher Friesem And Nir Davidson
abstract: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are challenging due to difficulties in tuning site connectivity, isolating local interactions, and mitigating finite-size effects. In this work, we experimentally investigate percolation with a platform of coupled lasers, where connectivity, interaction strength, and system size can be controlled. Using a square array of lasers with astronomical number of possible cluster configurations, we show that the emergence of a percolating cluster corresponds to the onset of phase locking among the lasers. We also show that the percolation probability undergoes a second-order alike transition as a function of the site-occupation probability, with a threshold consistent with classical theoretical predictions. Surprisingly, we find that at low pump level, amplified mode competition (nonlinear regime) alters the effective behavior of the lasing sites and modify the nature of the percolation transition. The experimental results are interpreted by the means of a theoretical toy model with connectivity rules to the classical percolation.
tldr: This paper experimentally studies percolation using a coupled laser array, showing that the percolation transition corresponds to phase locking and that nonlinearities modify the transition.
motivation: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are difficult; coupled lasers offer a tunable platform to investigate percolation dynamics.
method: A square array of coupled lasers with controllable connectivity and pump levels is used to observe percolation and phase locking, with a toy model to interpret results.
result: Percolation probability undergoes a second-order-like transition consistent with classical theory, but nonlinearities at low pump alter the transition.
conclusion: Coupled lasers provide a versatile experimental platform for percolation, revealing nonlinear effects that modify the phase transition.

title: Nonreciprocal Electrical Transport In Emerging Noncentrosymmetric Systems: From Hidden Symmetry To Functional Devices
authors: Shengyao Li, Zherui Yang, Xueyan Wang, Kian Ping Loh And X Renshaw Wang
abstract: Contrary to the reciprocal electrical transport constrained by the Onsager relations, nonreciprocal electrical transport arises in noncentrosymmetric systems where the resistance depends on the direction of current flow or external stimuli such as a magnetic field. Governed by symmetry-dependent charge dynamics, these responses appear as nonreciprocal charge transport (NCT) in the longitudinal direction and the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) in the transverse direction. Recent theoretical advances have expanded the range of mechanisms and material platforms capable of hosting nonreciprocal signals, revealing the role of hidden band-geometric properties. In parallel, experimental developments have exploited these effects for practical devices, offering promising alternatives to semiconductor-based rectifiers and wireless components, with advantages in broadband operation, ultrafast response, and high energy efficiency. In this review, we summarize electrical measurement techniques and characteristic transport signatures for identifying nonreciprocal phenomena and uncovering their underlying symmetry. We provide a comprehensive discussion of the fundamental mechanisms underlying NCT and NLHE, organized through representative material systems, and a subsequent examination of strategies for artificially inducing and enhancing nonreciprocity. Finally, we evaluate the technological perspectives of nonreciprocal electrical transport for electronic applications, along with key challenges and opportunities for scalable device implementation. By synthesizing current progress, this review aims to guide materials discovery and device innovation, and to inspire exploration of new symmetry settings and unconventional routes toward enhanced nonreciprocal functionalities.
tldr: A review of nonreciprocal electrical transport in noncentrosymmetric systems, focusing on symmetry-dependent charge dynamics and device applications.
motivation: To understand and harness nonreciprocal transport phenomena for next-generation electronic devices beyond conventional semiconductors.
method: Summarizes experimental techniques and theoretical mechanisms for nonreciprocal charge transport and nonlinear Hall effect across various material systems.
result: Identifies hidden band-geometric properties and symmetry conditions that enable nonreciprocity, and demonstrates proof-of-concept devices with broadband, ultrafast, and energy-efficient operation.
conclusion: Nonreciprocal electrical transport offers a promising route for functional devices, but challenges remain in materials discovery and scalable implementation.

title: Crystallography-driven Molecularization Of A Two-dimensional Spin- 3 / ...
authors: Hari Borutta, Tobias Müller, Ronny Thomale, Harald O Jeschke And Yasir Iqbal
abstract: Large-spin two-dimensional magnets are generally expected to develop conventional long-range order once the dominant exchange scale becomes appreciable. The layered spin- maple-leaf compound Na Mn O defies this expectation: despite sizable antiferromagnetic interactions and no evident disorder, it exhibits no magnetic ordering and displays two well-separated thermodynamic crossover scales. We show that this behavior originates from a crystallography-driven molecularization of the magnetic degrees of freedom. The low-symmetry structure partitions the Mn sublattice into inequivalent exchange pathways, generating a pronounced hierarchy that nearly isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons. Magnetic correlations therefore develop in two stages: first within individual hexagons at a scale set by the dominant exchange, and only at much lower temperatures do frustrated inter-hexagon couplings attempt to establish coherence across the lattice. While isolated hexagons reproduce the two-step thermodynamic structure, the experimentally relevant temperature scales emerge only once the hexagons are embedded in the frustrated two-dimensional network. The resulting quantum ground state is magnetically disordered, characterized by strong intra-hexagon correlations and rapidly decaying inter-hexagon correlations. These results identify crystallographic inequivalence as a materials-level mechanism for stabilizing molecularized and quantum-disordered states even in large-spin two-dimensional magnets.
tldr: This paper explains the absence of magnetic order in a large-spin 2D magnet via crystallography-driven molecularization into weakly coupled antiferromagnetic hexagons.
motivation: To understand why the layered spin-3/2 compound NaMn2O4 does not magnetically order despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions and no disorder.
method: The authors perform electronic structure calculations and model the magnetic system as a Heisenberg model on the maple-leaf lattice, analyzing exchange hierarchies and using classical Monte Carlo and exact diagonalization.
result: The low-symmetry crystal structure creates a hierarchy of exchanges that nearly isolate antiferromagnetic hexagons, leading to two-stage magnetic correlations and a quantum-disordered ground state.
conclusion: Crystallographic inequivalence can stabilize molecularized and quantum-disordered states in large-spin 2D magnets, offering a new materials-level mechanism for frustration.

title: Layerwise Stratification And Band Reordering In Twisted Multilayer MoTe2

SignificanceMultilayer graphene moiré systems have revealed rich correlated and topological quantum phases, yet twisted transition metal dichalcogenides have been studied mainly as bilayer. Here we show that adding more layers changes the underlying ...
tldr: This paper studies layerwise stratification and band reordering in twisted multilayer MoTe2, a material physics topic without direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To understand how adding more layers changes the electronic structure and correlated phases in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides beyond bilayers.
method: Theoretical modeling and possibly first-principles calculations to analyze band structure and layer-dependent effects in twisted multilayer MoTe2.
result: Layerwise stratification and band reordering are observed, altering the moiré potential and correlated phases.
conclusion: Multilayer twisted TMDs exhibit richer physics than bilayers, but the work is primarily materials science without quantum information or thermodynamics implications.

title: Continuous Thermochemical Sources Of AlF Molecules
authors: Pulkit Kukreja, Priyansh Agarwal, Maximilian Doppelbauer, Jionghao Cai, Xiangyue Liu, Eduardo Padilla, Sebastian Kray, Henrik Haak, Russell Thomas, Stefan Truppe, Boris G Sartakov, Gerard Meijer And Sid Wright
abstract: The AlF molecule, currently subject to laser cooling and trapping efforts, has the advantage that it can be efficiently produced in a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal. Here we present a series of experiments with continuous molecular beam sources of AlF, utilizing this reaction. We demonstrate a compact AlF molecular beam oven whose total far-field brightness is molecules per steradian per second at 923 K, just below the melting temperature of aluminum metal. The continuous output from the oven begins to exceed the peak brightness of a jet-cooled, ablation-based supersonic AlF source for the , level, and we obtain an excellent signal-to-noise ratio with the oven in pulsed laser ionization spectroscopy experiments. By delivering flux from the oven into a cryogenic Ne buffer gas cell, we lower the rotational temperature of the beam to around 30 K and reduce its most probable forward velocity from 600 m s to 200 m s . In addition, we demonstrate that AlF can be made in a simple dispenser package, and observe that molecules thermalize to the laboratory temperature after colliding with vacuum chamber walls of the experiment. The resulting transient AlF vapor may enable direct loading of a molecular magneto-optical trap.
tldr: This paper presents experimental demonstrations of continuous thermochemical sources for producing AlF molecules, focusing on molecular beam brightness and cooling for laser cooling and trapping.
motivation: AlF molecules are promising for laser cooling and trapping, but efficient and continuous sources are needed for advanced experiments.
method: The authors use a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal to produce AlF, and characterize the molecular beam using spectroscopy and buffer gas cooling.
result: They achieve a compact oven with high brightness, continuous output exceeding pulsed sources, and demonstrate rotational cooling to ~30 K using a cryogenic buffer gas cell.
conclusion: Continuous thermochemical sources of AlF are viable and can enable direct loading of magneto-optical traps, advancing molecular quantum science.

title: Distinguishing Near- Versus Off-critical Phase Behaviors Of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
authors: Gaurav Mitra, Souradeep Ghosh, Kiersten M Ruff, Ruoyao Zhang, Gaurav Chauhan And Rohit V Pappu
abstract: Intrinsically disordered prion-like low complexity domains (PLCDs) drive phase transitions that underlie the biogenesis of many biomolecular condensates. Here, we report results from large-scale Monte Carlo simulations on lattices aided by computations of Binder cumulants and rigorous finite-size scaling. These approaches enable accurate mapping of the critical regime and computations of the full binodal of an archetypal PLCD. This weakly associating polymer undergoes phase separation coupled to percolation. Between the lowest temperature and the critical point, the concentrations along the left arm of the binodal vary by four orders of magnitude. The overlap line intersects the left arm of the binodal well below the critical point. This, taken together with the intersection of the percolation line and the left arm of the binodal, leads to demarcation of the binodal into three regimes. Regime I is farthest from the critical point. Here, the coexisting dilute phase is akin to a gas of dispersed polymers. The dilute arm of the binodal lies above the overlap line in Regimes II and III. Here, the semidilute nature of dilute phases enables clustering of polymers that is enhanced by intermolecular associations. The coexisting dense phases form confined percolated networks in Regimes I and II. In Regime III, which is closest to the critical point, the dense phase becomes unconfined and fragmented, and the system is defined by two interconnected, system-spanning networks. In addition to mapping the critical point accurately, we evaluated methods for identifying the theta temperature. We find that scaling approaches based on assumptions from two-parameter theories for homopolymers yield erroneous estimates of the theta temperature of an archetypal PLCD. abstract: Heteroepitaxy on nanocrystals of diverse crystal structures—hexagonal close-packed (hcp), body-centered cubic (bcc), and face-centered cubic (fcc)—is a powerful approach for engineering atomic arrangements. abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations.
